glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
oxford-mission-church.desc: The Oxford Mission came to Barishal in the early 20th century, and its church, the Epiphany Church, is one of the largest in Bangladesh. Built of red brick with arched windows and a high bell tower, it feels unexpected amid the city's river bustle. The compound is shaded by tall trees and kept peaceful. Visitors are welcome with permission.
blocks: How to get there
In Barishal city; any rickshaw can take you.
Good to know
Ask at the gate before entering and keep voices low.

glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
karapur-miah-bari-mosque.desc: This mosque in North Karapur is said to have been built in the late 18th or early 19th century by Hayat Mahmud, a local zamindar who was exiled to Penang for resisting the British and built it after his return. Its design follows the Kartalab Khan Mosque in Old Dhaka: the prayer hall sits on a raised platform reached by a wide stair, with rooms below now used as a madrasa. Three ribbed domes crown the roof, the middle one larger, and the white walls carry fine floral plasterwork. A pond lies in front. It is protected by the Department of Archaeology but sees few visitors from outside.
blocks: How to get there
From Barishal city take an auto to Karapur via Kashipur or Nabagram crossroads (about 20–30 min).
Good to know
It is an active mosque, so dress modestly and avoid prayer times. Late afternoon light on the white facade and pond is lovely.

glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
qasba-mosque-gournadi.desc: Qasba was an important Muslim settlement in the Sultanate period, and its mosque dates from the early 16th century, in the time of Alauddin Husain Shah. Nine domes sit on thick brick walls, with corner towers and terracotta work around the arches, much like the Nine Dome Mosque in Bagerhat. Locals often credit it to the Mughal faujdar Sabi Khan, but historians place it earlier. The mosque is still used for daily prayers and is protected by the Department of Archaeology. It is one of the oldest standing buildings in greater Barishal.
blocks: How to get there
Take any Dhaka-bound bus from Barishal's Nathullabad terminal and get off at Gournadi; the mosque is in Qasba village by the highway, a short rickshaw ride away.
Good to know
It is an active mosque: dress modestly, remove shoes, and avoid prayer times. Women may be asked to view from outside.

glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
guthia-mosque.desc: Known officially as Baitul Aman Jame Masjid, the Guthia Mosque was completed in the early 2000s on the Barishal–Banaripara road. Its white dome and slender minaret stand beside a big pond, with palm-lined walks and flowerbeds around it. Inside, the hall is cool and richly decorated. At sunset the reflection in the water draws many visitors.
blocks: How to get there
About 20 km from Barishal city; take a bus or auto towards Banaripara and get off at Guthia.
Good to know
Dress modestly; women may have restricted access to some parts during prayers.

glance: Sweet shops at Gournadi bus stand
gournadi-doi.desc: Gournadi upazila is famous for its sweet curd, set slowly in clay pots until firm enough to cut. It has a creamy texture and caramel sweetness. Buses on the highway often stop here so travellers can buy pots to take home. It is eaten after meals or with chira and muri.

glance: Deck approx. 300–500 BDT, cabins approx. 1,200–5,000 BDT
dhaka-barishal-launch.desc: For generations, the people of the south have travelled to Dhaka and back on large multi-deck launches. They leave Sadarghat in the evening, cross the Meghna under the night sky and dock at Barishal around dawn. Passengers sleep in cabins or on mats on deck, with tea sellers and food stalls on board. Even with the new Padma Bridge roads, the journey remains a loved part of river culture.
blocks: Good to know
Book cabins early around holidays; avoid travel when storm signals are raised; keep belongings secure on deck.

glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
durgasagar-dighi.desc: Durgasagar at Madhabpasha in Babuganj was dug in the late 18th century by a local raja and named after his mother. It is one of the largest ponds in southern Bangladesh, with a small tree-covered island in the middle and walkways around the banks. In winter, migratory ducks rest on the water. Families come for picnics and boat rides.
blocks: How to get there
About 11 km from Barishal city by auto or bus on the Banaripara road.
Good to know
Go in the morning in winter to see birds before the crowds arrive.

glance: Varies with size and season, approx. 900–2,000 BDT per kg
Fish markets and riverside hotels in Barishal city
barishal-ilish.desc: The Meghna, Tentulia and other rivers around Barishal are among the main hilsa grounds of Bangladesh, and the national fish is part of daily life here. Fresh ilish is cooked in shorshe ilish, with a mustard paste, fried crisp with its oil poured over rice, or steamed in banana leaf. The fat, sweet flesh is at its best in the monsoon season. The city's fish markets and river hotels make it an obvious place to try it.

bibir-pukur.desc: Bibir Pukur is an old rectangular pond in central Barishal, dug in the 18th century and named after a local woman remembered for it. Today it is the city's living room, with a paved path, lights and benches around the water. In the evenings people stroll, chat and snack from nearby stalls. It is an easy place to feel the city's pace.
blocks: How to get there
In the city centre near Sadar Road; walk or take a rickshaw.
Good to know
Evening is liveliest; try local snacks around the edge.

glance: Homes in Barishal during Ramadan, and traditional food fairs in Barishal city; ask locals, as shops rarely sell it
barishal-molida.desc: Molida is Barishal's own Ramadan drink. Soaked rice is ground fine and mixed with soft puffed and flattened rice, milk, fresh grated coconut, a little ginger and sugarcane jaggery, then served in a glass, cool or warm. Not long ago many Barishal homes made it every day of Ramadan; today it is rarer, and you are most likely to find it in family kitchens and at traditional food fairs.

glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
mahilara-sarkar-math.desc: Mahilara Math was built in the mid-18th century, during Nawab Alivardi Khan's rule, by a local notable named Rupram Das Gupta. The octagonal spire rises roughly 27 metres above its base and is decorated with stucco, terracotta and rows of curved cornices. Over time the tower has tilted southward by about five degrees, which is why locals call it the 'helano math'. It survived attacks in 1971 and later, and is now a protected monument of the Department of Archaeology. It stands in open village surroundings and takes only a short while to see.
blocks: How to get there
From Barishal take a bus towards Gournadi on the Dhaka–Barishal highway, get off at Mahilara, then a short rickshaw or auto ride to the temple.
Good to know
Combine it with the Qasba Mosque, also in Gournadi, a few kilometres away. Morning or late-afternoon light shows the tilt best in photos.

glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
lakutia-zamindar-bari.desc: The Lakutia zamindar family was founded by Rupchandra Roy, and his grandson Rajchandra Roy built the main house on a large estate in Lakutia village. The family is also remembered in Barishal for building the road to the city and founding Rajchandra College. The surviving mansion has two storeys and nine rooms, surrounded by three paved ponds known as Babur Pukur. Part of the land is now used by the agricultural development corporation (BADC). In 2025 the Department of Archaeology began restoring the building, so expect scaffolding while work goes on.
blocks: How to get there
From Barishal city take an auto or rickshaw along Lakutia Road (about 30 min). Durgasagar Dighi is a short ride away.
Good to know
Combine with Durgasagar on the same half-day. Ask before entering any part under restoration.

glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
sher-e-bangla-museum-chakhar.desc: Chakhar in Banaripara is the ancestral village of A. K. Fazlul Huq, the statesman remembered as Sher-e-Bangla. The Department of Archaeology built a museum on part of his homestead, and it opened in 1983. Its two galleries show family photographs, newspaper clippings and his personal things, including an armchair, bed, dressing table and walking stick. There are also older relics such as a black stone Shiva linga, a statue of Marichi and old coins. The quiet village setting, with the school and college that carry his name, is part of the visit.
blocks: How to get there
From Barishal city take a bus or auto on the Banaripara road and get off at Chakhar (about 1 hr); the museum is a short walk from the bazar.
Good to know
Government museums are usually closed one or two days a week, so check locally before making the trip. Guthia Mosque lies on the same road and makes an easy pairing.

glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
satla-shapla-bil.desc: Around Satla in Wazirpur, low-lying beels fill with water each monsoon and then bloom with water lilies, the national flower. In the early morning the surface turns red and white as far as you can see. Local boatmen paddle visitors through narrow channels between the flowers, and farmers collect lily stems to sell as vegetables. It is a seasonal sight that rewards an early start.
blocks: How to get there
From Barishal, travel to Wazirpur by bus, then onward to Satla by local transport.
Good to know
Arrive before 9 am when flowers are open; respect farmers' collecting areas.

glance: 180 km to Barishal by road, 5–6 hours by bus or car
sugandha-shaktipeeth.desc: Hindu tradition counts 51 Shakta pithas, places where parts of the goddess Sati's body are said to have fallen, and Sugandha at Shikarpur is one of them. The temple here is dedicated to the goddess Sunanda. Her Bhairava, Tryambak, has his own temple at Ponabalia near Jhalokathi on the Sugandha river. Pilgrims come all year, and the biggest gathering is on Shiva Chaturdashi.
blocks: How to get there
Take a bus, CNG or auto from Barishal north towards Wazirpur and get off at Shikarpur; ask locals for the Sugandha temple.
Good to know
Shiva Chaturdashi (February–March) is the festival day; expect large crowds. Remove your shoes in the temple and follow the priests' guidance.
